atom: QG-35b: the price of SELECTION and of ACTIONABILITY, against identification
freeze: development/orion-qg-regime-geometry/QG35B_SELECTION_PRICE_FREEZE_V1.md, committed before the solver ran, with definitional pins and four admissible branches
outcome_branch: B1 -- D_sel* = 3, so the committed QG-35(c) STANDS and the coarsening 715 -> 646 buys nothing
the_new_content: the worst case is 3 for all three targets, but the ACTIONABLE problem is strictly easier in DISTRIBUTION: more than twice as many free starting states (16 vs 7) and less than half as many worst-case states (7 vs 16), with 26 of 92 classes strictly cheaper

three_targets.actionable: resolve until the INTERSECTION of the remaining optimal-frame sets is nonempty, i.e. until one frame is known to be optimal for every candidate still in play -- what a compiler actually needs
three_targets.identification: resolve to a single orbit type (QG-34's target)
three_targets.selection: resolve until all remaining types share the SAME optimal-frame set (frozenset equality, pinned in the freeze -- not overlap, not lex-min agreement)

verification.cap_soundness: solver C caps at depth 3, which is sound because singletons are terminal for all three targets, so any identification tree is a valid selection and actionable tree: D_act <= D_sel <= D_id
verification.infeasibility_certificates: cert_all true on both frozen solvers
verification.solver_b: best-first probe ordering with branch and bound
verification.solver_c: research/extensions/orion-qg/qg35b_independent_third_solver.py -- iterative deepening on sorted tuples, written independently in the main session

why_actionable_is_the_right_target: a compiler does not need the input's identity, nor the full set of optimal frames -- it needs one frame it can commit to. That is a weaker stopping condition and it is NOT a partition target, so it needed its own recursion rather than a coarsening
